prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Pavement slipp’ry, people sneezing, Lords in ermine, beggars freezing; Titled gluttons dainties carving, Genius in a garret starving. Lofty mansions, warm and spacious; Courtiers cringing and voracious; Misers scarce the wretched heeding; Gallant soldiers fighting, bleeding. Wives who laugh at passive spouses; Theatres, and meeting-houses; Balls, where simp’ring misses languish; Hospitals, and groans of anguish. Arts and sciences bewailing; Commerce drooping, credit failing; Placemen mocking subjects loyal; Separations, weddings royal. Authors who can’t earn a dinner; Many a subtle rogue a winner; Fugitives for shelter seeking; Misers hoarding, tradesmen breaking. Taste and talents quite deserted; All the laws of truth perverted; Arrogance o’er merit soaring; Merit silently deploring. Ladies gambling night and morning; Fools the works of genius scorning; Ancient dames for girls mistaken, Youthful damsels quite forsaken. Some in luxury delighting; More in talking than in fighting; Lovers old, and beaux decrepid; Lordlings empty and insipid. Poets, painters, and musicians; Lawyers, doctors, politicians: Pamphlets, newspapers, and odes, Seeking fame by diff’rent roads. Gallant souls with empty purses; Gen’rals only fit for nurses; School-boys, smit with martial spirit, Taking place of vet’ran merit. Honest men who can’t get places, Knaves who shew unblushing faces; Ruin hasten’d, peace retarded; Candor spurn’d, and art rewarded.

outputs.L3:
Society is portrayed as deeply unequal, divided between a privileged elite and a suffering majority. While the wealthy enjoy comfort, luxury, and influence, beggars remain destitute, soldiers endure hardship, and talented individuals receive little recognition or support. Wealth and status, rather than service or ability, determine who prospers.

This inequality is reinforced by widespread corruption and greed. Courtiers, misers, rogues, and dishonest officials flourish because they know how to manipulate the system for personal advantage. Meanwhile, honest people and those of genuine merit are ignored or pushed aside. Success no longer reflects virtue, talent, or public service; instead, it rewards flattery, selfishness, and deceit.

Cultural and intellectual life suffers under the same distorted values. Artists and authors struggle to survive, even as fools dismiss genius and mediocrity wins public approval. Truth, judgment, and good taste are abandoned in favor of fashionable opinions and shallow entertainment. As a result, creativity is undervalued, intellectual standards decline, and society loses the ability to distinguish lasting achievement from empty display.

Economic and political conditions also reveal a broader national decline. Commerce weakens, public credit collapses, and tradespeople struggle to maintain their livelihoods. Rather than addressing these urgent problems, political leaders act irresponsibly: they postpone peace, pursue damaging policies, and accelerate the country’s movement toward ruin. Private hardship and public mismanagement thus become closely connected.

Social life, meanwhile, is depicted as superficial and absurd. Gambling, vanity, frivolous amusements, and the behavior of idle aristocrats dominate public attention. Ambition is directed toward titles, appearances, and social advancement rather than useful or honorable goals. Taken together, these conditions present a society in moral, cultural, economic, and political decay—one in which wealth is celebrated over virtue, folly over wisdom, and spectacle over substance.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a sweeping and sharply satirical survey of British society, moving rapidly between public institutions, political life, commerce, religion, domestic relationships, and fashionable social circles. By placing sharply contrasting scenes beside one another, it exposes the gulf between society’s professed ideals and its actual conduct. Poverty exists alongside luxury, genuine ability is neglected while mediocrity is rewarded, and public virtue repeatedly serves as a disguise for private greed. Politicians pursue influence rather than the common good; corruption and self-interest shape public decisions; religious and moral language conceal hypocrisy; and social status is valued more highly than integrity or compassion. Even private life reflects the same distorted priorities, as relationships are governed by money, ambition, and appearance rather than loyalty or affection.

Across this catalogue of abuses, the poem suggests that injustice is not accidental but deeply embedded in the social order. Wealth can purchase respectability, power can silence criticism, and deceit often proves more useful than honesty. Those with genuine merit, wisdom, or creative genius are overlooked unless they possess the patronage and influence needed to succeed, while flatterers, opportunists, and frauds prosper. The result is a world in which moral values have been reversed: vice receives the rewards that should belong to virtue, and outward success is mistaken for true worth. The poem’s conclusion therefore extends beyond ridicule into warning. A nation that consistently prefers wealth to merit, influence to justice, and falsehood to truth undermines its own stability. By rewarding corruption and frustrating honesty, it accelerates social and political decline, deepens conflict, and prevents the establishment of genuine peace.
outputs.L5:
## Lords of the Pavement

At dawn, the city belonged to the pavement lords—couriers, buskers, vendors, and wanderers who knew every crack in the concrete. None were titled by kings, yet each carried an invisible crown shaped by endurance. They ruled no palaces, only street corners glowing beneath tired lamps, where stories were traded for coins and kindness.

By noon, polished shoes hurried past without noticing them. But when evening settled over the rooftops, music rose from the pavement, warm and defiant. For a moment, the city remembered its true nobility: not those born into privilege, but those who made a kingdom from whatever ground remained beneath their feet.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write out the full text of “January, 1795” by Mary Robinson, omitting the title and author’s name.
counterfactuals.output:
Pavement slipp’ry, people sneezing,  
Lords in ermine, beggars freezing;  
Tartars plenty, Frenchmen many,  
Stout of heart, and light of penny.

Mansions mighty, servants witty,  
Many a heart, and many a city;  
Country healthy, London airy,  
Convents empty, castles dreary.

Knaves in office, statesmen jarring,  
Nations mad, and monarchs warring;  
Earthquakes, wars, and conflagrations,  
Speechifying, proclamations.

Ancient ladies, young beaux leading,  
Clerks and judges, trials pleading;  
Rats and mice by cats tormented,  
House and furniture distrained.

Poets, painters, and musicians,  
Doctors, lawyers, politicians;  
Pamphlets, newspapers, and odes,  
Seeking fame by different roads.

Gallant soldiers fighting, flying,  
English sailors conquering, dying;  
Fame, by getting killed and dying,  
Honour purchased, truth expiring.

Bankers, brokers, overflowing,  
Little fortunes daily growing;  
Rapid carriages, slow coaches,  
Noisy cits, and silent roaches.

Asses, bears, and bulls, and horses,  
Marshals, generals, different forces;  
Patriots preaching, factions brewing,  
Lord knows what the nation’s doing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me the satirical eighteenth-century poem that contrasts aristocratic luxury with poverty, featuring the lines “Genius in a garret starving” and “Honest men who can’t get places.”
counterfactuals.output:
The poem is **“A Description of London,” an anonymous eighteenth-century satire** (sometimes confused with John Bancks’s poem of the same title). The relevant passage reads:

> Houses, churches, mixed together,  
> Streets unpleasant in all weather;  
> Prisons, palaces contiguous,  
> Gates, a bridge, the Thames irriguous;  
>   
> Gaudy things enough to tempt ye,  
> Showy outsides, insides empty;  
> Bubbling trades and mechanic arts,  
> Coaches, wheelbarrows, and carts;  
>   
> Lords in coaches, beggars craving,  
> **Genius in a garret starving;**  
> Ladies richly dressed in satins,  
> Rogues in rags and fools in patterns;  
>   
> Places given to blockheads’ graces,  
> **Honest men who can’t get places;**  
> Wealth and title, pride and pelf—  
> London’s world all in itself.

Several versions circulated, so wording and attribution vary between collections.
